A tertiary amino compound that is N,N-dimethylethanamine substituted at position 1 by a 1-hydroxycyclohexyl and 4-methoxyphenyl group.
A glucose metabolism disease that is characterized by high blood glucose.

A molecular process that can be carried out by the action of a single macromolecular machine, usually via direct physical interactions with other molecular entities. Function in this sense denotes an action, or activity, that a gene product (or a complex) performs.

A biological process is the execution of a genetically-encoded biological module or program. It consists of all the steps required to achieve the specific biological objective of the module. A biological process is accomplished by a particular set of molecular functions carried out by specific gene products (or macromolecular complexes), often in a highly regulated manner and in a particular temporal sequence.

Any process that is carried out at the cellular level, but not necessarily restricted to a single cell. For example, cell communication occurs among more than one cell, but occurs at the cellular level.
Catalysis of the transfer of a phosphate group, usually from ATP, to a substrate molecule.
The initial attachment of a membrane or protein to a target membrane. Docking requires only that the proteins come close enough to interact and adhere.
The human gut microbiome transforms and degrade drugs using enzymes.
A drug is any substance that causes a change in an organism's physiology or psychology when consumed or introduced.

An agent that kills a virus or that suppresses its ability to replicate and, hence, inhibits its capability to multiply and reproduce. For example, amantadine (Symmetrel) is a synthetic antiviral. It acts by inhibiting the multiplication of the influenza A virus.
The primary factors that determine the drug metabolism.
The main mechanisms of drug modification, inactivation of a drug, and drug degradation.
The categories to group enzymes into gene families, mechanisms, and drug classes.

Among the molecules directly targeting viruses, nucleoside analogues form an essential class of broad-spectrum antiviral drugs. Many direct-acting antiviral nucleoside analogues target the viral polymerase responsible for the viral genome replication. Unlike non-nucleoside polymerase inhibitors that often bind to allosteric non-conserved and mutation-tolerant sites, nucleoside analogues directly bind to the more conserved active site of the viral polymerase after conversion to their triphosphate active form. Nucleoside analogs represent the largest class of small molecule-based antivirals, which currently form the backbone of chemotherapy of chronic infections caused by HIV, hepatitis B or C viruses, and herpes viruses.

The enzymes which catalyze the reversible phosphorolysis of pyrimidine nucleosides are involved in the degradation of these compounds and in their utilization as carbon and energy sources, or in the rescue of pyrimidine bases for nucleotide synthesis.
A gene family is a set of several similar genes with respect to structure, function, and origin.
Any chemical reaction or series of reactions, often enzyme-mediated, which result in a physiologic effect.
The process of rendering antiviral medication ineffective. This can be done through various mechanisms.
The process of breaking down antiviral agents.
The process of breaking down antineoplastics agents.
The process of rendering anitineoplastic medication ineffective. This can be done through various mechanisms.

The central nervous system agents are medicines that affect the central nervous system (CNS). There are many different types of drugs that work on the CNS, including anesthetics, anticonvulsants, antiemetics, antiparkinson agents, CNS stimulants, muscle relaxants, narcotic analgesics (pain relievers), nonnarcotic analgesics (such as acetaminophen and NSAIDs), and sedatives. Features of CNS drugs are related to their ability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier affinity and exhibit CNS activity and can be used in the management of neuro degenerative and psychiatric problems.
A chemical compound that participates in a chemical reaction that produces dopamine.

Tyrosine decarboxylase (TDC) is an enzyme with the ability to decarboxylate L-tyrosine into tyramine. Due to the structural similarities between tyrosine and levodopa, TDC found in small intestinal bacteria can convert levodopa to dopamine. Moreover, commonly used decarboxylase inhibitors, carbidopa, benserazide, and methyldopa, do not inhibit TDC. This reduces the efficacy of the drug since the conversion of levodopa to dopamine occurs outside the brain.
A group of therapeutics targeting the heart.
A specific bacterial enzyme that allows E. lenta bacteria to metabolize and deactivate digoxin.

This gene is responsible for encoding proteins which are homologous to bacterial cytochromes, this allows the bacteria to use digoxin as an alternate electron acceptor.  Cgr1 is not directly involved in digoxin reduction, instead, it has a more general function such as electron transfer, or membrane docking. The function of cgr1 is thought to be completing the electron transfer from a membrane-associated electron donor (e.g. the membrane quinone pool) to the [4Fe-4S] cluster of the Cgr2 reductase via its covalently bound heme groups. It is highly up-regulated by digoxin and other cardiac glycosides containing unsaturated butyrolactone rings, such as digitoxin, digoxigenin, and, to a lesser extent, ouabain. It is repressed by arginine but not by ornithine. It is a part of an operon that consists of cgr1 and cgr2.

This gene is involved in the inactivation of the cardiac medication and plant natural product digoxin, thus decreasing drug efficacy and toxicity. It catalyzes the reduction of the alpha,beta-unsaturated butyrolactone ring of digoxin to the inactive metabolite dihydrodigoxin. It likely uses the cytochrome Cgr1 as the physiological electron donor, encoded by the adjacent gene in the locus. cgr2 only reduces digoxin and other cardenolide toxins, such as digitoxin, digoxigenin, ouabain and ouabagenin. Therefore, it is a specialized enzyme present in some gut bacteria E. lenta that protects their human host against ingested plant toxins.

Beta-glucuronidases are members of the glycosidase family of enzymes that catalyze breakdown of complex carbohydrates. Bacterial beta-glucuronidase can metabolize to 18-beta-glycyrrhetinic acid (GA) as a main product and to 18-beta-glycyrrhetinic acid-3-O-beta-D-glucuronide (GAMG) as a minor product.

The uridine phosphorylase catalyzes the reversible conversion of uridine to uracil and ribose-1-phosphate in bacteria. This enzyme efficiently deglycosylates capecitabine, deoxyuridine, and doxifluridine.
A pyrimidine deoxyribonucleoside that is a pyrimidine ribonucleoside in which the hydroxy group at the 5' position is replaced by a hydrogen.
A drug class is a set of medications and other compounds that have similar chemical structures, the same mechanism of action, a related mode of action, and/or are used to treat the same disease.

Products made from botanicals, or plants, that are used to treat diseases or to maintain health are called herbal products, botanical products, or phytomedicines. A product made from plants and used solely for internal use is called an herbal supplement.

Antineoplastic drugs (ANDs), also known as cytostatic drugs, are a heterogeneous group of chemicals used to control the growth of neoplastic cells. Most ANDs interfere with cell proliferation through DNA destruction, RNA synthesis, or duplication process. Unfortunately, ANDs do not distinguish cancer cells from normal ones, leading to unwanted adverse effects in patients receiving chemotherapy. The International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC) classifies some ANDs as human carcinogens.

Topoisomerase inhibitors are chemical compounds that block the action of topoisomerases. Topoisomerase plays key roles in cellular reproduction and DNA organization, as they facilitate the cleavage of single and double stranded DNA to relax supercoils, untangle catenanes, and condense chromosomes in eukaryotic cells. Topoisomerase inhibitors affect these essential cellular processes by preventing topoisomerases from performing DNA strand breaks or prevent the re-ligation step of the topoisomerase mechanism by interacting with topoisomerase-DNA complexes. These topoisomerase-DNA-inhibitor complexes are cytotoxic agents because the un-repaired single and double stranded DNA breaks that they cause can lead to apoptosis and cell death. Due to this ability to induce apoptosis, topoisomerase inhibitors have gained interest as therapeutics against infectious and cancerous cells.

Camptothecin (CPT) is a topoisomerase inhibitor. It was discovered in 1966 during a systematic screening of natural products for anticancer drugs. It was isolated from the bark and stem of Camptotheca acuminata (Camptotheca, Happy tree), a tree native to China used in traditional Chinese medicine. CPT has showed anticancer activity in clinical trials, especially against breast, ovarian, colon, lung, and stomach cancers. To maximize the therapeutic effects, four CPT analogues have been approved and are used as antineoplastic agents.

A member of the class of pyranoindolizinoquinolines that is the carbamate ester obtained by formal condensation of the carboxy group of [1,4'-bipiperidine]-1'-carboxylic acid with the phenolic hydroxy group of (4S)-4,11-diethyl-4,9-dihydroxy-1H-pyrano[3',4':6,7]indolizino[1,2- hydrochloride]quinoline-3,14-dione. Used (in the form of its hydrochloride salt trihydrate) in combination with fluorouracil and leucovorin, for the treatment of patients with metastatic adenocarcinoma of the pancreas after disease progression following gemcitabine-based therapy. It is converted via hydrolysis of the carbamate linkage to its active metabolite, SN-38, which is ~1000 times more active.
These are enzymes responsible for the breakdown and utilization of nucleosides.

Thymidine phosphorylase (TP) enzyme catalyzes the phosphorolysis of the nucleosides thymidine (dThd) and deoxyuridine (dUrd) to the corresponding bases thymine and uracil, and deoxyribose-1-phosphate. Thymidine phosphorylase (TP), is also related to Pyrimidine nucleoside phosphorylase (PYNP), which catalyzes the reversible phosphorolysis of pyrimidines in the nucleotide synthesis salvage pathway. In lower organisms (e.g. Bacillus stearothermophilus) PYNP accepts both thymidine and uridine, whereas in mammalian and other higher organisms it is specific for thymidine (designated thymidine phosphorylase, TP). Non-proton pumping type II NADH dehydrogenase (NDH-2) plays a central role in the respiratory metabolism of bacteria, and in the mitochondria of fungi, plants and protists. The lack of NDH-2 in mammalian mitochondria and its essentiality in important bacterial pathogens suggests these enzymes may represent a potential new drug target to combat microbial pathogens. NADH dehydrogenases ensures adequate oxidation of NADH to NAD+. Most species possess one to two isozymes of the non-proton-translocating type 2 dehydrogenase (Ndh), also termed alternative NADH dehydrogenase. While complex I is deeply integrated into the inner membrane, alternative NADH dehydrogenases are not membrane-embedded, but rather associated to the membrane surface, either on the IMS side (external NADH dehydrogenases) or the matrix side (internal NADH dehydrogenases). Unlike complex I, alternative NADH dehydrogenase lack flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and iron-sulfur clusters as reactive groups. Instead, they contain a flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD) cofactor to mediate the electron transfer from NAD(P)H to ubiquinone. Alternative NADH dehydrogenase can serve as important valves on the respiratory chain when oxygen tensions suddenly rise. NADH dehydrogenases also serve as as ‘apoptosis inducing factors’ in a poorly understood process that involves the formation of a toxic protein fragment on the outside or inside of the mitochondrial outer membrane and in animals but not in yeast, AIFM1 serves as biogenesis factor for MIA40 and thus, indirectly, for many IMS proteins.

DHDR requires NADPH as a cofactor but not NADH, possibly explained by the presence of the arginine (R64) residue. In the case of DHDR from S. isoflavoniconvertens, the tyrosine of most of the known SDR family enzymes seems to be replaced with histidine, for which imidazole ring (de)protonation would be engaged in substrate reduction or oxidation. DHDR is involved in the reduction of (S)- and (R)-dihydrodaidzein, (S)- and (R)-DHD,  to trans- and cis-tetrahydrodaidzein (trans- and cis-THD), respectively.

Escherichia coli thioesterase I (TAP) is a versatile enzyme possessing activities of thioesterase, esterase, arylesterase, protease, and lysophospholipase. It has been documented with three different names, including thioesterase I, protease I and lysophospholipase L1, which are responsible for the degradation of thioester, amide, and ester bonds. E. coli thioesterase I, first identified by Barnes & Wakil, was cloned in 1993 and shown to catalyze hydrolytic cleavage of acyl-CoA thioesters. At the same time, protease I, named for its hydrolytic activity toward N-acetyl-dl-phenylalanine-2-naphthyl ester, was also cloned and characterized. Lysophospholipase L1, which catalyzes the hydrolysis of 1-acyl group of lysophospholipid was purified and its DNA sequence deduced in 1999. Recent studies showed that the gene sequences of E. coli thioesterase I (tesA), protease I (apeA) and lysophospholipase L1 (pldC) were identical and located at the same genomic position. Also, substrate competition assays showed that thioesterase I and protease I utilize the same active site, and all of them were identified as periplasmic proteins. The most plausible physiological role of TAP is that of lysophospholipase L1, since TAP shows specificity towards lysophospholipids and its activity on 1-acyl lysophosphatidylcholine follows typical Michaelis–Menten kinetics. TAP has stereoselectivity for amino acid derivative substrates, hence it is useful for the kinetic resolution of racemic mixtures of industrial chemicals.

The core of each enzyme is similar: an alpha/beta sheet, not barrel, of eight beta-sheets connected by alpha-helices. These enzymes have diverged from a common ancestor so as to preserve the arrangement of the catalytic residues, not the binding site. They all have a catalytic triad, the elements of which are borne on loops which are the best-conserved structural features in the fold. The alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes are one of the largest known protein families, including lipases, esterases, amidases, epoxide hydrolases, dehalogenases and hydroxynitrile lyases. The alpha/beta-hydrolase fold consists of eight beta-strands connected by alpha-helixes. These fold into a mostly parallel central beta-sheet surrounded by alpha-helixes. The catalytic triad consists of a nucleophile (serine, aspartate or cysteine), a histidine and a catalytic acid (aspartate or glutamate). These residues occur on conserved locations in loops and the alpha/beta-hydrolase fold brings them together to form the active site. Many alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes also contain cap domains, the structures of which vary considerably between the different members. A cap domain sits on top of the active site, which is in the alpha/beta-hydrolase domain. In spite of their similar three-dimensional structures and similar active site residues, alpha/beta-hydrolase fold enzymes catalyse reactions with substrates containing a broad variety of functional groups, including carboxylic acid derivatives (esters, amides and thioesters), epoxides, alkyl halides and hydroxynitriles. The common mechanistic feature of these reactions is a nucleophilic attack.

Phenothiazines belong to the oldest synthetic antipsychotic drugs, which do not have their precursor in the world of natural compounds. Apart from their fundamental neuroleptic action connected with the dopaminergic receptors blockade, phenothiazine derivatives also exert diverse biological activities, which account for their cancer chemopreventive-effect, such as calmodulin- and protein kinase C inhibitory actions, anti-proliferative effect, inhibition of P-glycoprotein transport function and reversion of multidrug resistance.

The pfkB family of enzymes across kingdoms includes ribokinases, phosphofructokinases, adenosine kinases (ADKs) and several others with diverse substrate specificities. Typical PfkB protein structure is a large domain consisting of a beta-sheet sandwiched between several alpha-helices, and a smaller domain, known as the lid domain, comprised of another beta-sheet attached to the larger domain by short loops that act as a hinge. Binding of substrates to pfkB proteins follows ordered bi-bi kinetics where the carbohydrate enters first, followed by ATP. PfkB proteins possess two signature motifs: a di-gly (GG) motif in the N-terminal region and a G/AXGD motif in the C-terminal region. The role of each motif has been identified through mutational and structural analyses. The GG motif provides flexibility in the hinge region that connects the lid and the large domain. The aspartate in the G/AXGD motif acts as a base during catalysis and activates the C6 fructose hydroxyl group for nucleophilic attack on the gamma-phosphate in ATP. Many pfkB proteins are active as dimers generated through interactions between the lid domains of two monomers. Aside from their regulation by ATP, pfkB family enzymes are activated by both monovalent and divalent cationic cofactors.

Cyclomaltodextrinase (CDase) is a maltogenic amylase and neopullulanase are reported to be capable of hydrolyzing all or two of the following three types of substrates: cyclomaltodextrins (CDs); pullulan; and starch.

Glycoside hydrolases (GHs) (EC 3.2.1.X) hydrolyze glycosidic bonds between carbohydrates or between carbohydrate and non-carbohydrate components, for instance alcohols or phenols. To date, enzyme classification is based on amino acid similarities rather than substrate specificity. GHs are assigned to different groups based on conserved domains, and the families are numbered from 1 to 131 that are listed in the Carbohydrate-Active Enzymes Database. Family GH13, also known as the alpha-amylase family, is the largest sequence-based family of glycoside hydrolases and groups together a number of different enzyme activities and substrate specificities acting on alpha-glycosidic bonds.

Phospholipid N-methyltransferase (PLMT) enzymes catalyze the S-adenosylmethionine-dependent methylation of ethanolamine-containing phospholipids to produce phosphatidylcholine. Phosphatidylcholine is the most abundant phospholipid in most non-plastid membranes of eukaryotes and functions as a structural membrane lipid, and as a precursor to important lipid-based signaling molecules. In mammals and fungi, phosphatidylcholine can be formed through two distinct pathways: (a) the “nucleotide pathway” in which free choline is incorporated in phosphatidylcholine using CDP-choline as an intermediate, and (b) the “methylation pathway” whereby phosphatidylcholine is produced directly from phosphatidylethanolamine (PtdEtn) via three sequential methylation reactions using S-adenosylmethionine (AdoMet) as the methyl donor. In plants, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis occurs through a branched pathway that utilizes components of both the nucleotide and methylation pathways. In mammals, the 18-kDa integral membrane protein phosphatidylethanolamine N-methyltransferase (PEMT) is a PLMT that is expressed primarily in the liver. PEMT catalyzes all three of the methylation reactions needed to convert PtdEtn to phosphatidylcholine.

Analgesics are the drugs which bring insensibility to pain without loosing consciousness. Treatment strategy is generally based on the type of pain. Most of the analgesics are associated with serious side effects, such as NSAIDS can cause severe GI disturbance and opioids can cause addiction.

Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) is a cofactor for about 4% of all biochemical reactions. PLP and five other ‘vitamers’, are collectively known as vitamin B6. In general, there are two independent de novo pathways that generate PLP: the deoxyxylulose 5′-phosphate (DXP)-dependent pathway, which is present in most eubacteria (e.g. Escherichia coli), and the ‘DXP-independent’ route, which is widespread (e.g. some eubacteria, Archaea, fungi and plants) and consists of a single enzyme complex, PLP synthase. In the PLP salvage pathway, however, different vitamers are interconverted using various kinase, phosphatase and pyridoxine/pyridoxamine 5′-phosphate oxidase (PNPOx) enzymes. The reaction catalysed by members of the PNPOx family (so-called PdxH proteins) is equivalent to the last step of the DXP-dependent PLP biosynthesis pathway, oxidizing either PNP or PMP to produce PLP. Members of the family utilize flavin mononucleotide (FMN) as a prosthetic group, oxidizing the C4′ alcohol (PNP) or amine (PMP) group to an aldehyde (PLP). During catalysis, FMN is used as the immediate electron acceptor and molecular oxygen as the final electron acceptor, forming hydrogen peroxide under aerobic conditions. Pyridoxal 5′-phosphate biosynthesis is essential for the survival and virulence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the organism that causes tuberculosis (TB) and is, for this reason, an important drug target at a time when resistance is rising and new drugs are urgently needed.

Catechol O-methyltransferase catalyzes the methylation reaction whereby a methyl group from the cofactor S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is transferred to one of the catecholic hydroxyls. Membrane-bound form COMT (MB-COMT) may be more relevant in inactivation of catecholaminergic neurotransmitters, whereas the soluble form (S-COMT) plays a more important role in inactivation of endogenous and xenobiotic catechols in other tissues. COMT is the primary enzyme that inactivates the catechol neurotransmitter dopamine and the drug L-dopa. L-dopa is used in the clinical treatment of central nervous system (CNS) disorders such as Parkinson's disease and possibly others (e.g. schizophrenia and depression). Its efficacy is associated with the level of dopamine converted from the drug. Studies have shown that inhibition of COMT activity results in marked reduction of the body clearance of L-dopa and dopamine, leading to a sustained level of dopamine in the brain and improved efficacy. The important role of COMT in treatment of Parkinson's disease has promoted an area wherein the aims are to design potent and selective COMT inhibitors. Several of these inhibitors have been used as adjuncts to L-dopa therapy.

Histamine is primarily found in mast cells and basophils, where it is stored in cytoplasmic granules and released along with other inflammatory mediators upon activation in response to diverse immune and non-immune stimuli, including viruses and other pathogens. Histamine exerts multiple (patho)physiological actions by activating four known types of histamine receptors that are designated as H1–H4 and have been associated with allergic inflammation, stimulation of gastric acid secretion, neurotransmission and immune responses, respectively. This led to drugs, such as H1 antihistamines for the management of allergies, H2 receptor antagonists for the treatment of gastrointestinal disorders, a first-in-class H3 receptor antagonist for treating narcolepsy, as well as H4 receptor-targeting compounds that are being evaluated in clinical trials for their potential exploitation in managing inflammatory disorders.

One particular transcription factors (TF), the fumarate and nitrate reductase regulatory protein (FNR), is among the most widely studied global regulators, activating and repressing transcription of a wide variety of functional genes. FNR is widely conserved across bacteria and is often required for the shift between aerobic and anaerobic metabolism. FNR belongs to the catabolite repressor protein (CRP; also known as cAMP receptor protein)/FNR family of TFs, which plays an important role across bacteria and generally shares a conserved DNA binding site. Like FNR, CRP is well studied and widely conserved across bacteria and responds to variations in glucose availability via changes in the concentration of cyclic AMP. Besides CRP and FNR, the CRP/FNR family of proteins contains other well-studied TFs that respond to a variety of environmental stimuli.
